articles.author: aws@amazon.com
articles.body: Bulletin ID: 2026-181-AWS Publication Date: 11/12/2026 13:00 PM PST Description: We identified CVE-2026-127119, an issue in the EMR module of AWS SDK for pandas (awswrangler) from version 1.1.0 before 3.18.0. When a cluster is created without an explicit log location, the library uses a predictable default S3 bucket name for the cluster logs without verifying that the caller's account owns that bucket. A remote actor who creates that bucket first could read the cluster's logs, including job step output. Impacted versions: >= 1.1.0 AND < 3.18.0 Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.

articles.body: Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs? That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries. Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams. More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning. The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together. What this looks like in practice Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations. 3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work...

articles.title: Trained to betray: How post-training supply chain attacks hijack coding agents
articles.summary: Microsoft Defender Research and the AI Red Team discuss how poisoned datasets and poisoned model checkpoints can trigger remote code execution and other malicious activities. The post Trained to betray: How post-training supply chain attacks hijack coding agents appeared first on Microsoft Security...
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Microsoft AI Red Team, Amanda Minnich, Amit Eliahu, Blake Bullwinkel, Dor Edry and Giorgio Severi
articles.body: In this article Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse toolsModel poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transferWhat the studies show about agent backdoorsMitigation and protection guidanceSecuring agents beyond the modelReferences Learn More As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why. A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access. First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness. Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses. These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools. Introduction Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. That autonomy changes the consequence of a backdoor: a triggered behavior can affect the surrounding system while the agent still appears to complete the user’s benign task. The trigger itself may not look malicious. It can be an ordinary user request...

articles.author: Alysa Taylor
articles.body: Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC, commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain. In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale. What the research found Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters. Measurement is the next test. Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms. Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks. Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy. “Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC. AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses. Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability. Where scale stalls 66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them. The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design. Inside the Frontier Firm IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in...

articles.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
articles.summary: Threat actors are deploying GSocket on compromised Linux servers to keep encrypted remote access after the original vulnerability is patched. Learn how to detect, investigate, and remediate this activity. The post The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2 appeared...
articles.author: Yash Gund, Sumith Maniath and Microsoft Security Research
articles.body: In this article When one RCE stops being just one RCEObserved attack chainsHow threat actors deploy and operate GSocketHow GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 addressMitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn More Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it. To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions. GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it. Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself. articles.body: In this article From scans to reportsSelected findingsClosing thoughts At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab, we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline. Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers. In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI. From scans to reports We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. Code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6 (71.1% of code-scanning tokens), GPT-5.4 (20.1%), and GPT-5.5 (7.1%). The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two weeks on two servers (64 cores/256 GB RAM and 32 cores/128 GB RAM), but turning that output into patches and reports took months of expert work. articles.title: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
articles.summary: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons to inject a short payload; Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous...
articles.author: Microsoft Threat Intelligence
articles.body: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models. Key findings from Microsoft Research include: Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post. A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment. The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it. Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously. Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code. Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Learn more from the Microsoft Research Blog: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming dormant neurons to backdoor AI agents Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to defend against this threat as part of a broader defense-in-depth approach. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions. Audit model weights before deployment and after every update Diff every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update....

articles.body: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? articles.title: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust
articles.summary: Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers found memory-safety bugs in Rust's core and std libraries, including cases where safe Rust code can trigger undefined behavior. Using Hyenas, FORGE's frontier research version of codename MDASH, the team investigated three patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code...
articles.author: Yechan Bae and FORGE Lab
articles.body: In this article How we found and validated the bugsPattern 1: Trusting code not to panicPattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correctPattern 3: Trusting the underlying systemWhy Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AIRust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent. Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate. Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today. In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. articles.author: Ben_Harris
articles.body: Earlier this year, we introduced the Protection & Posture Insights report: an on-demand, tenant-specific view of the email & collaboration threats targeting your organization, how well Microsoft Defender is stopping them, and where your configuration can be strengthened. Today, we're announcing the latest updates to the report, shaped directly by your feedback. Here are the highlights: URL Protection: visibility beyond the inbox Attackers follow users wherever they work. Malicious links now show up in Teams conversations, Office files and Microsoft 365 Copilot responses as well as email, and many look harmless until after they're delivered. Microsoft Defender checks links when users click them, and the new 'URL Protection' insight shows how many clicks were checked, how many attempts to reach malicious sites were blocked, and how that activity breaks down across email, Office apps, Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Filtering Overrides: find the exceptions weakening your posture Allow lists and transport rules are sometimes needed for business continuity, but every exception can weaken your protection. The new 'Filtering Overrides' insight shows how many phish, malware and spam messages were permitted by organization-level and user-level overrides, and which override types were responsible. It also flags overrides applied to messages Defender had already classified as clean, a strong signal that they can be retired. Where an override is genuinely required, we recommend the Tenant Allow/Block List, which offers more visibility, auditing and control than broad transport rules. Go Hunt: increased coverage Our 'Go Hunt' experience opens Advanced Hunting with the exact query behind an insight, so you can explore and customize the underlying data yourself. It's now available on more insights, including URL Protection, Filtering Overrides and Detection Trends, so you can dig as deep into the data as you need. Get started Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 customers can generate the report in a couple of minutes. In the Microsoft Defender portal, go to Reports -> Email & collaboration reports. Then select 'Generate' on the Protection & Posture Insights report card. You can also go directly to the Reports page within the Microsoft Defender portal. Learn more about email & collaboration reports with our documentation. We'd love to hear what you think about the report, and what you'd like to see next. articles.title: New investments to reduce on-premises security risk
articles.summary: We’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, bringing together guidance, migration, and product investments. The post New investments to reduce on-premises security risk appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Paul Lorimer
articles.body: On-premises servers can be essential to business operations, but they are increasingly attractive targets to attackers. AI can help less-skilled actors analyze software, develop malicious tools, and repeat attack workflows at greater speed and scale, shortening the window between exposure and exploitation. Organizations need to strengthen security faster without disrupting the critical workloads they rely on. Today, we’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, initially focused on server workloads. The initiative brings together guidance, migration, and product investments to help customers understand and prioritize risk, reduce their on-premises footprint wherever possible, and strengthen critical workloads that need to remain. Guidance for the initiative will soon be available through Secure Now, which also includes our AI readiness checklist in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and guidance for strengthening foundational security. Understand Identify the most important on-premises risks and prioritize actions customers can take now. Reduce Move workloads to Microsoft 365 where possible to take advantage of cloud-based security, resilience, and continuous innovation. Secure Strengthen critical workloads that need to remain on-premises and reduce the manual work required to keep them secure. This approach starts with understanding where to focus—and extends to making supported on-premises products more secure by default. Modernize where you can, and strengthen the security of what must remain. Making supported on-premises workloads more secure by default Within the Secure pillar of the on-premises security initiative, we’re also hardening the products themselves through On-Premises Baseline Security Mode, starting with supported Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server workloads. On-Premises Baseline Security Mode On-Premises Baseline Security Mode is designed to make the default security posture stronger—reducing the number of recommended security settings administrators must configure and maintain manually. For supported on-premises server workloads, it starts with a validated and tested secure-by-default configuration from initial deployment, while preserving administrator control. articles.body: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available. Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts. Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC. Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

articles.body: In this article Attack chain overviewMitigation and protection guidanceLearn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms. This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity. articles.body: In this article Classifying the vulnerability landscapeVulnerabilities exploited in the wildWhere defenders should focusPatching is slow, while exploitation is fastImpact, exposure and where to focusNext in lineHow Microsoft Security helps defenders actReferencesLearn More The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data...

articles.author: yuvalpery
articles.body: Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 (Brotli releases). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (Node.js security release). If you can't patch your applications right away, Azure WAF on Application Gateway, Application Gateway for Containers and Azure Front Door can help mitigate the inbound attack vector, which is Brotli-compressed request bodies sent to your application. Note: Azure WAF inspects only inbound requests to your application. It can't protect applications that fetch and decompress Brotli-encoded responses from external servers. Those applications must be patched. Built-in protection enabled by default If you use Azure WAF with DRS 2.2 on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door Premium, you're protected by default against crafted Brotli-compressed request bodies. Rule 920450 (Paranoia Level 1, enabled by default) checks requests against a list of restricted headers, and DRS 2.2 adds Content-Encoding to that list. The rule has a critical anomaly score, so a single match blocks the request when the WAF policy is in Prevention mode. Earlier rule set versions don't restrict the Content-Encoding header. If you're still on DRS 2.1, CRS 3.2 or earlier, we recommend upgrading to DRS 2.2 to get the latest protection. To learn how, see Upgrade CRS or DRS ruleset version. If your application uses Next.js image optimization, apply the BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 custom rule below, even if you're on DRS 2.2. CVE2026111497 blocks any request whose Content-Encoding header includes the br (Brotli) coding, which this attack uses. DRS 2.2 already covers this vector through rule 920450. articles.author: MaximeBombardier
articles.body: In April, I published a set of referential architecture diagrams for Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Purview Referential Architecture Diagrams. They have been useful in workshops and training sessions for a simple reason: one picture is worth a thousand words - attempting to explain the complex in a single image. Today I'm publishing an update focused on classification and labeling — and on the wave of public previews that make auto-labeling something you can scale across the entire estate with ease. ➡️ Download the interactive architecture on GitHub here. It's a self-contained HTML file - and it's a lot more than this picture! Why now: auto-labeling scales to the whole estate The most consequential change is surprisingly small. An auto-labeling policy can now be kept on while you edit it, without re-triggering simulation. Anyone who has run auto-labeling at scale knows why that matters. Until now, tuning a policy meant turning enforcement off, re-simulating, waiting, and turning it back on — delays every time you refined a rule. That friction made it challenging for organizations from broadening scope as fast as they wanted to. Removing it changes the operating model: you can simulate once with your conditions and expand scope (sites) when you're ready, without hitting the simulation limit. It arrives alongside a set of previews that lift every ceiling that used to cap the motion: Capacity is up 5x. Auto-labeling for SharePoint and OneDrive moves from 100,000 to up to 500,000 files per tenant per day (Roadmap ID 567890). Simulation goes from 4M to 20M items, so you can model against a real estate rather than a sample. Policy scope gets much bigger. Select up to 1,000 individual SharePoint sites per policy, adaptive scopes support up to 50,000 sites, and you can filter sites by the SiteTemplate property when configuring a policy (Roadmap ID 570445, MC1469958). Reporting finally tells you what happened. Audit and reporting now summarize the sensitive information types detected when labels are applied, and a new 30-day chart shows files processed per day so you can watch policy throughput. A per-policy coverage report correlates files processed during enforcement to the latest simulation run — including the files that enforcement processed but simulation never saw (Roadmap ID 568935). articles.body: Welcome back to What's new in Microsoft Sentinel. In October, cross-tenant delegated access reaches general availability so you can run security operations across tenants with least privilege, the Advanced Security Information Model (ASIM) EmailEvent schema gives you one consistent structure for email events across sources, an SAP analytics rule helps you spot active use of custom apps with high or critical vulnerabilities, and Unified Data Management brings connectors, tables, and ingestion health together in the Microsoft Defender portal. Read on for the details, and don’t forget to register for our upcoming Microsoft Ignite conference below in additional resources. Sentinel innovations: Sentinel SIEM Sentinel data lake Sentinel SIEM Cross-tenant delegated access (Generally available) Cross-tenant delegated access in Defender lets you run security operations across tenants using the same governance relationship model as Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance. articles.summary: Teams support impersonation led to remote access, malicious runtime execution, and Certificate Services abuse through authentication relay and Kerberos. The post From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Sagar Patil, Jesse Birch and Tal Tzhori
articles.body: In this article Activity overviewAttack chain overviewPortable runtime staging and execution variantsHost discovery and AD CS assessmentCase 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusionCase 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identityWhy the response outcomes differedActionable investigation methodsReferencesLearn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths. Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication). This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations. articles.body: As local agents have moved from experimentation into everyday work, traditional security visibility is no longer enough. Unlike static software, local agents such as coding assistants, command-line agents, desktop applications, and agentic development environments can operate on endpoints with access to a user's data, credentials, tools, and services. They can also connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that extend their access to additional tools and data. This change requires security teams to look beyond. Today, discovery of AI agents and their configured MCP servers on Windows and macOS is generally available, with discovery coverage expanded to more than 50 supported agents and MCP servers. On eligible, onboarded devices, Defender discovers supported agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context together to give security teams visibility for their local agent environment. Beyond discovery, runtime protection for local agents for Windows continues to be available in preview, helping protect discovered agents as they operate. Teams can deploy runtime protection at scale from either the Microsoft Defender portal or the Microsoft Intune portal, with Intune-based deployment available in preview. Both discovery and runtime protection for local agents will be available for Microsoft Defender for Endpoint P2 and higher customers. See the local agents and associated MCPs operating in your environment In the Defender portal, security teams can see the discovered agents under Assets. The inventory associates each agent with the device and user account where it runs and includes details such as agent name, version, vendor, related process, and discovery history. articles.title: Defending Linux in the age of AI-operated attacks
articles.summary: Linux supports cloud services, containers, developer environments, business-critical applications, and a growing share of AI infrastructure. That makes Linux both essential to modern enterprises and increasingly attractive to attackers. AI is compressing the time required to research targets, vary...
articles.author: tejaskashyap
articles.body: Linux supports cloud services, containers, developer environments, business-critical applications, and a growing share of AI infrastructure. That makes Linux both essential to modern enterprises and increasingly attractive to attackers. AI is compressing the time required to research targets, vary payloads, and adapt when an attempt fails. Customers need protection that can recognize modern attacker behavior at runtime, continuously test effectiveness against realistic attacks, and learn and evolve with the threat landscape. That’s why Microsoft Defender is focused on three priorities for Linux: stronger runtime protection for fileless and in-memory attacks, continuous validation that proves protection remains effective, and AI-powered defense that can help security teams simulate attacks, investigate threats, close protection gaps, and reduce exploitable paths before compromise. A new Linux threat model The threat landscape has evolved from AI-assisted attacks, where people use AI to accelerate individual tasks, to AI-operated attacks, where AI coordinates more of the attack chain, and now it is moving to autonomous AI attacks that can adapt and act with limited human direction. Modern Linux attacks rarely depend on one file; they combine exposed services, stolen credentials, legitimate administration tools, scripts, containers, and cloud-native attack paths. As AI helps attackers generate and modify payloads at scale, adapt when an attempt fails, and move through the attack chain faster, defenders can no longer assume that every payload, script, or binary will resemble something they have seen before. Microsoft Security Research recently observed compromises involving a LiteLLM gateway, a RAGFlow deployment, and a Kestra workflow environment. The intrusion paths differed, but the objectives converged around credential theft, persistence, downstream access, and compute monetization. The broader lesson is that AI gateways, retrieval platforms, and orchestration services are becoming high-value control points where data, credentials, model connectivity, and workload execution meet. These examples also highlight a broader shift: attackers increasingly abuse legitimate services, tools, and workflows rather than relying solely on overtly malicious binaries. Viewed one event at a time, Bash, Python, curl, SSH, and network connections can appear legitimate. The security challenge is to understand their sequence, process relationships, destinations, and runtime...

articles.body: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-41709 Broadcom VMWare ESX Insufficient Logging Vulnerability CVE-2026-46300 Linux Kernel Missing Initialization of a Variable Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.author: IustinIrimia
articles.body: Attacks rarely stay in one channel. A flood of spam email, a Teams chat from an unfamiliar organization, and a call from "the helpdesk" can all be part of the same attempt. Security teams need a unified way to see where attacks are happening across email and collaboration, investigate them quickly, and show whether their defenses and users are improving. That's the job of our Detections and Insights reports. They're ready-to-use templates that turn Defender's email and collaboration data into views your team can use every day, as a Microsoft Sentinel workbook or a Power BI report. Today we're releasing version 4, which builds on Part 3 of this series, with new hunting queries and a new report for attack simulation training. Shaped by customer feedback, it helps you: See the attacks that matter with new Teams and impersonation views. Investigate faster with 125 new or improved hunting queries. Measure and improve resilience with a new attack simulation training report. See the attacks that matter In September, Microsoft Threat Intelligence described a campaign that starts on Teams: an attacker from another organization poses as IT support in a chat or call and talks the user into a remote session. Spotting activity like this early means looking at Teams alongside email. The new Teams & Collaboration view puts those Teams signals in one place: threats in chats and channels, callers and senders with support-style names such as "IT Helpdesk", new external senders, risky links, and the calls and messages users reported. A new Email – Impersonation & BEC tab in the workbook does the same for email, highlighting impersonation attempts that reached an inbox and the people they targeted. Each major workbook tab now opens with key numbers and recommended actions, so the team can go from "what happened?" to "what should we check next?" in one place. In Microsoft Sentinel, the workbook can also combine several workspaces in one view, which helps managed security service providers (MSSPs) and organizations with many tenants. The Teams & Collaboration view and the Email – Impersonation & BEC tab, shown with test data from a lab tenant. Investigate faster When something needs a closer look, the next questions come quickly. Has this sender contacted us before? Did anyone report a call from them? Are several addresses using the same "IT Helpdesk" display name? To help answer them, we added 71 new hunting queries for email and collaboration and improved 54 existing ones....

Now password-only users can go straight to a passkey, making it easier to adopt strong authentication from day one. As part of this work, we will also be enabling Authenticator App passwordless sign-in to be a user's first registered MFA method. articles.body: Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, shared the below communication with Microsoft employees today. Today, we’re introducing a new Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to eligible employees within participating organizations. This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs. The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program. What employees should know This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below. This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs. Eligible employees will receive an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details within the next few hours. Looking ahead The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute. My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving. Thank you for everything you continue to do for our customers, Microsoft and for one another. articles.summary: Hi all. Jerry Devore dropping in for a minute to share some insights about the BlockNtlmv1SSO setting that went into effect with the October 2026 update. Why the change was necessary When MS-CHAPv2 is used for solutions like VPN, Wi-Fi, NPS, and RADIUS, the authentication flow leverages the MD4...
articles.author: JerryDevore
articles.body: Hi all. Jerry Devore dropping in for a minute to share some insights about the BlockNtlmv1SSO setting that went into effect with the October 2026 update. Why the change was necessary When MS-CHAPv2 is used for solutions like VPN, Wi-Fi, NPS, and RADIUS, the authentication flow leverages the MD4 hash of the account’s password to respond to a challenge. If that sounds familiar, then you have at least a basic understanding of NTLM. The problem is that this relic from 1998 (NT 4.0 SP4) produces a response to the challenge that is cryptographically equivalent to NTLMv1. So, while a device using MS-CHAPv2 can have NTLMv1 disabled, it is still exposing the same type of challenge response that makes NTLMv1 trivial to crack. The Change B ack in August 2025, an update added support for the registry setting BlockNtlmv1SSO (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0). The update did not create the registry setting, but it caused devices to start auditing for the use of "NTLMv1-derived credentials". With the October 2026 update, the default for Windows devices is to block the use of NTLMv1-derived credentials. This means that organizations that are still dependent on CHAPv2 are going to be impacted. Bracing for Impact For organizations that have already blocked NTLMv1 in their domains, there is no required action because MS-CHAPv2 using domain credentials is already impossible. For everyone else, you might want to do your due diligence before letting the October update rip if you are not certain whether you have any dependencies on MS-CHAPv2. The documentation for this change mentions events 4024 (Warning) and 4025 (Error) which are logged to the NTLM log of the client (Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational). Those events are extremely helpful, but very few organizations are forwarding the client NTLM logs to their SIEM. Possibly a better approach The October 2026 update giveth and the October update taketh away. What do I mean by that? Besides taking away NTLMv1-derived credentials, the update backported the enhanced NTLM auditing events to Server 2019 and Server 2022. As a result, you can leverage your domain controllers’ logs to determine if you have any MS-CHAPv2 dependencies prior to updating your endpoints. Here is an example of a 4033 event logged on a domain controller when the VPN server forwarded the challenge response for "credential validation". This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. YouTube Video Click here to load media A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. articles.body: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful. While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents. Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted. This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised. Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise. They are agentic insiders. Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly. To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7. An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime. In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise. articles.body: As more developers begin to use Linux desktops, they become more attractive to attackers: high-privilege, high-value, and easy for admins to overlook. A developer using Linux for day-to-day development may interact with source code repositories, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, cloud infrastructure, container environments and internal development platforms. If their workstation is compromised, an attacker doesn’t just gain access to a laptop, but a foothold in the pipelines that build and ship the organization’s software. As Linux adoption expands beyond the data center, organizations need a consistent approach to protecting Linux wherever it is used. That’s why we’ve extended our industry-leading endpoint protection in Microsoft Defender, bringing enterprise-grade protection, detection, vulnerability management and response capabilities to Linux workstations. Enterprise-grade protection for Linux desktops Defender support for Linux workstations spans all three key areas of endpoint security: Protect and detect Endpoint detection and response (EDR) Microsoft Defender next-gen antivirus Threat analytics Exposure management Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Device inventory Security settings management Investigate and respond Advanced hunting Live response Device isolation The result is broader Linux protection, delivered through the tools and processes security teams already trust. Give security teams a consistent and simplified view across the endpoint estate With Defender on Linux desktops, organizations can: Onboard quickly using the deployment methods already validated for Linux servers Reduce operational complexity by protecting Linux desktops and servers with one agent and one security operations experience Improve visibility across heterogeneous endpoint environments Strengthen developer workstation security where users interact with source code, cloud infrastructure and other critical resources Accelerate investigation and response through a consistent security operations experience Defender protects Linux desktops with the same deployment organizations already use to protect Linux servers.
